summary:
North Maluku is a province of Indonesia and stands under the national framework. Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors: the national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual sexual activity between adults outside marriage. Because Indonesia does not permit same-sex marriage, the provision reaches every consensual same-sex relationship, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Where an immediate family member lodges a complaint, unmarried partners face up to one year's imprisonment.

North Maluku has no separate criminalisation statute, no separate document regime and no recorded deviation from national policy material enough to score it apart. The Sharia-based criminalisation outlier in Indonesia is the province of Aceh, whose punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present there; two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in Aceh in February 2025. Nothing in the sources places equivalent provincial powers in North Maluku.

Document rules are national. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option, and legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery together with a judge's approval.

Physical risk is rising across the country. International reporting in August 2026 describes growing repression of Indonesia's transgender community, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people while the government moves to codify anti-LGBT provisions; a presidential decree of October 2025 lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue, including the arrest of 75 people at a privately rented villa near Bogor on 22 June 2025.

No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution is silent on both. On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected a petition, by five votes to four, to criminalise homosexuality.
tangentialFactors:
Provincial religious law in Aceh shows how far sub-national units can depart from the national baseline in Indonesia, a departure North Maluku does not share. Visitors should read Aceh as a distinct legal zone rather than as evidence about North Maluku.

Official posture runs against protection. Indonesia voted against the creation of a United Nations independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, and a 2023 Pew Research survey found 95% of Indonesians oppose same-sex marriage. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge in mob attacks on transgender people directly to officials' public condemnations.

Adjacent national measures that bear on expression and association: the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment, the national broadcasting commission banned presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal in March 2016, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying gay-related content. A bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour was under discussion in 2025.
localsOnly:
Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians electronic ID cards in nine provinces, which is the functioning document route alongside the surgical-and-judicial recognition requirement.

The national constitutional framework contains no protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution itself does not address either. Residents therefore rely on ordinary criminal and civil provisions rather than on specific equality guarantees.

Custody risk is documented nationally: in August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, and Indonesian police denied that violence was used.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: sources give different maximum terms for the outside-marriage provision, one reporting up to two years' imprisonment and another up to one year where an immediate family member complains. The relationship between the two figures is not sourced here.

Not sourced: whether the nine-province electronic ID card outreach includes North Maluku, and whether the nine provinces are named in any source in this inventory.

No North Maluku-specific evidence of enforcement, police raids, mob attacks or local regulation was available. The province entry in the source inventory carried no usable finding, so the assessment rests entirely on the national framework and the national pattern of repression.

Not sourced: whether North Maluku applies any provincial religious bylaw of the kind Aceh uses, or whether Indonesian immigration screening at entry asks questions capable of disclosing a visitor's gender history.
